items.title: Start with the alphabet
items.body: Learn the 26 handshapes of the fingerspelling alphabet and spell your own names. Fingerspelling is used for names, places and words without a sign of their own. Practice reading words with the fingerspelling page on this site.

items.title: Work through Lifeprint's free lessons
items.body: Dr. Bill Vicars, a Deaf ASL professor, teaches 60 free lessons at Lifeprint (ASL University), each with videos, vocabulary and practice sentences. ASL 1 is Lessons 1–15, ASL 2 is 16–30, ASL 3 is 31–45, and ASL 4 (46–60) is practice sentences. One lesson a week, with a few minutes of practice each day, is a good pace for a family. The lesson planner can lay them out week by week.

items.title: Watch stories told in ASL
items.body: Children pick up a language from stories. The American Society for Deaf Children keeps a free directory of hundreds of children's books retold in ASL, and Gallaudet's Clerc Center has a free app of picture books translated into ASL.

items.title: Look up signs as you need them
items.body: When you want a sign for something in your day, look it up in a video dictionary and use it right away. Signs are easiest to remember when you use them for real things at home.

items.title: Learn about the Deaf community
items.body: ASL belongs to the Deaf community, and learning it includes learning about the people who use it. The National Association of the Deaf explains why ASL matters and where it comes from.
